title: Westbrook City Council — Regular Meeting

fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)

note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. Summarization necessarily condenses and selects; for complete context, nuance, and anything not covered here, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: President Jennifer Munro, Vice President Michael Shaughnessy, Brian McCambridge, Victor Chau, Anna Turcotte, Gary Rairdon. Absent: Amy Faulkingham. Mayor David Morse also attended.

blocks.x: Mayor’s Message, Council Messages & First Public Comment
Routine Items: Pride Month, Alewife Migration, Police Staffing & Upcoming Topics
Discussion Summary
Mayor Morse proclaimed June 2026 as Pride Month in Westbrook. He cited the 1969 Stonewall riots and the City's support for its LGBTQIA+ community.

He announced that the annual alewife migration from Casco Bay through Mill Brook began the previous week. The Presumpscot Regional Land Trust is hosting guided viewing walks (details at prlt.org). Residents were asked to keep people and pets out of the cordoned-off fish-viewing pools.

He authorized a temporary increase in police staffing from 48 to 49 officers, starting in July 2026. This comes ahead of Captain David Thompson's September retirement. It lets a replacement hire start the police academy this summer, so there is no staffing gap. Authorized staffing goes back to 48 once Thompson retires.

Director of Planning and Code Enforcement Rebecca Spitella will repeat her recent Planning Board presentation on residential growth trends for the full Council on June 15. She will also give it separately to the School Committee.
The Mayor has directed staff to prepare data for a broader discussion later this year. That talk would be about a possible school impact fee, a fee on new development to pay for added public costs.

Public Safety Committee Chair Amy Faulkingham will chair a July 6 committee meeting. It will cover the City's current blanket ban on motorized scooters on public streets, to consider a repeal or revision.
Key Decisions
Informational — no vote taken.
Action Items
None.
Tribute to Retiring Former City Administrator Jerry Bryant
Discussion Summary

Mayor Morse gave a long, emotional tribute to former longtime City Administrator Jerre “Jerry” Bryant at his final Council meeting as a City employee. Bryant had worked for Westbrook for more than 23 years. The Mayor presented him with a ceremonial key to the city.
Bryant, replying at age 72, reflected on his time in the job. He credited the City's various mayors and councils for putting the City's interests ahead of personal disagreements.

Councilors Rairdon, Chau, Turcotte, and Shaughnessy and President Munro followed with personal tributes during Council Messages. These included Chau's and Turcotte's memories of Bryant guiding them as new councilors.

First Public Comment continued in the same vein. Assistant City Administrator Jennie Franceschi read a letter honoring his career from Bryant's high school (Oxford Hills Comprehensive, class of 1972, football standout). Brendan Riley, who served on the committee that hired Bryant, called it “the best decision we ever made”. Chris Dudley and Sue Joyce also offered thanks.
Key Decisions
Informational — no vote taken.

Orders of the Day — Second & Final Reading
Orders 2026-61, -62, -64 — Davan Pool, FD Donation & Trail Blazes Funding (Consent)
Discussion Summary
All three had their first reading (the first of two required votes) at the May 18, 2026 meeting. This is the second and final reading, the final, binding vote. The three items are listed here.
One is confirming the $8,348.30 Davan Indoor Pool emergency motor-repair expenditure.
Another is accepting a $5,000 Enbridge/American Online Giving Foundation donation plus a $6,850 Fire Department supply hose purchase.
The third is $30,000 in Recreation & Conservation Commission funding for Westbrook Trail Blazes trail-grooming equipment.
See that meeting's summary for full detail.

Order 2026-63 — Pyxis Medication-Storage Rental Agreement (Separated for Discussion)
Found on page 25 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

City Administrator Holmes asked that this item, first read May 18, be considered separately. Holmes disclosed a last-minute problem. The vendor (CareFusion Solutions) had said earlier that the five-year rental could be converted mid-agreement to an outright purchase. During the meeting itself, the vendor sent an email taking that assurance back.

Holmes said the Administration still recommended going ahead with the rental as presented. He noted that the Council could table the item (set it aside to take up later) for further vendor discussion if it preferred.

Councilor Chau asked that staff monitor the balance of opioid settlement funds, which pay for the item. He wanted a quick change of course if those funds run low before the rental's five-year term ends. The Council went ahead without tabling.
Key Decisions
Passed by unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.

New Business — Business License
Happy Wheels Skate Center — Liquor License (Public Hearing)
Found on page 45 of the packet. Public hearing held; no opposition.
Discussion Summary

Following a public hearing with no opposition, the Council approved a State Liquor License for Happy Wheels Skate Center (84 Warren Ave., Unit K). The license lets the four-year-old, family-owned rink add beer and wine service. Co-owner Taylor (with husband Derek Fitzgerald) noted that people had asked about the license since the business opened. Mayor Morse and Councilor Chau both praised the rink's “Kids Skate Free Club” affordable-access program and its popular school skate nights.
Key Decisions
Passed by unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.

Order 2026-65 — Annual Vendor List Amendment
Found on page 57 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

Amends the FY2025–2026 Annual Vendor List to add Northern Light Wellbeing, LLC (dba Work Health) as an approved vendor for occupational health services. These services are physicals, injury evaluations, and return-to-work assessments for the Fire, Police, and Dispatch departments. The existing vendor, Concentra Occupational Health, stays on the list. The change was made because demand for these services is rising.

Order 2026-66 — Data Center Moratorium Ordinance
Found on page 59 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

Enacts a 180-day moratorium on siting, permitting, construction, or operation of any data center in Westbrook. This gives staff time to review the Land Use Ordinance's current data-center provisions. Today those provisions only permit the use within the Rock Row contract zone (a special zoning deal for one property).

Councilor Turcotte asked what prompted this. Mayor Morse explained that Governor Mills vetoed a statewide data-center moratorium (Legislative Document 307). After that, state legislators urged municipalities to consider their own local moratoriums.

Around the same time, Westbrook learned that neighboring Scarborough had received an actual data-center application. This prompted the City to get its own policy in order before any proposal arrives here. No data center has been formally proposed in Westbrook.

Councilor Chau asked whether a data center could open simply because the ordinance does not address it. Assistant City Administrator Jennie Franceschi confirmed that data centers are not currently a permitted use anywhere in the City. The one exception is the Rock Row contract zone.
Councilor Turcotte asked that an attorney practicing in the artificial intelligence, information technology or information-security field review any draft ordinance language.
Discussion confirmed that the moratorium focuses on the impact of large-scale data centers on local electrical and water utility capacity. It does not focus on data or privacy concerns.

Councilor Chau separately noted, as an aside, a growing trend of small-scale compute and battery units being installed in private homes. He called it a related but distinct phenomenon worth future awareness.
Key Decisions
Passed by unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Victor Chau.
